articles.title: China, Asean pledge restraint as talks on South China Sea pact face key hurdles
articles.summary: China and Southeast Asian nations have pledged to avoid actions that could escalate tensions in the disputed South China Sea, as leaders met in Manila on
articles.body: China and Southeast Asian nations have pledged to avoid actions that could escalate tensions in the disputed South China Sea, as leaders met in Manila on Monday to push forward negotiations on a long-delayed code of conduct for the strategic waterway.The commitment is aimed at creating a more conducive atmosphere for negotiations on an agreement intended to prevent maritime disputes from spiralling into conflict. However, despite progress in the talks, differences over the proposed pact's scope and legal status remain unresolved.A draft joint statement seen by The Associated Press said China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) would pledge “to exercise self-restraint in the conduct of activities that would complicate or escalate disputes and affect peace and stability” in the South China Sea.The leaders were also expected to welcome the “positive momentum and significant progress” in negotiations and stress the need to maintain an environment conducive to reaching an agreement. A final joint statement had not been issued as of the time of this report.Chinese premier Li Qiang called for an early conclusion of the code of conduct, saying it could help promote peace and stability in the region, according to China's state news agency Xinhua. Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr, whose country holds Asean's rotating chairmanship this year, also pointed to progress made during the negotiations.Three major differences remainThe negotiations have been underway for more than two decades, with the sides agreeing in 2023 to try to conclude the code this year. But the deadline is now in doubt.Philippine foreign secretary Theresa Lazaro said the sides had agreed on around 80% of the proposed agreement's paragraphs, although three contentious issues remained. She said negotiations would continue next year, when Singapore takes over Asean's chairmanship.Lazaro had put the figure at 77% after ministerial meetings over the weekend, according to the South China Morning Post (SCMP).The main sticking points include the geographical area that the code would cover, the definition of sensitive terms and whether the agreement would be legally binding. The role of countries outside Asean and China is another point of disagreement.China has resisted Asean's push for legally enforceable provisions, while the Philippines wants the agreement to preserve the rights of countries that are not parties to it. Beijing, meanwhile, has sought restrictions on joint military exercises and energy exploration involving outside powers, SCMP reported.Geographical scope is particularly difficult because it touches on competing territorial claims. Bao Yinan, an associate research fellow at China's Huayang Centre for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance, told SCMP that including the disputed Paracel Islands would run counter to Beijing's position that there is no territorial dispute over the islands.Maritime confrontations complicate negotiationsThe diplomatic push comes amid recurring confrontations between Chinese and Philippine vessels in disputed waters, including near the Second Thomas, Scarborough and Sabina shoals. China, Taiwan and four Asean members – Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam – have competing claims in the South China Sea.The waterway is a major global trade route and a potential flashpoint between Beijing and Washington. The United States does not claim territory there but has a mutual defence treaty with the Philippines and has warned that an armed attack on Philippine forces could trigger its treaty obligations.The proposed code is intended to reduce the risk of such disputes escalating into a wider conflict. But analysts have warned that repeated confrontations have eroded trust between the countries involved, making diplomatic compromises harder to secure.Bao told SCMP that sustained clashes between China and the Philippines, both at sea and through public exchanges, had depleted mutual trust and could complicate negotiations.With Singapore set to take over Asean's chairmanship in 2027, the negotiations will continue under a new regional lead. Singapore, which is not a claimant in the South China Sea disputes, could help facilitate discussions, although its ability to influence the most contentious issues remains uncertain.The disputes have also drawn wider international attention because of the possibility that a major confrontation could involve the United States, a longstanding security ally of the Philippines.You use AI every day. articles.title: Manipur shuts down over killing of 4 Tangkhul Nagas
articles.summary: Manipur shutdown over Nov 13 killing of four Tangkhul Nagas; six Liangmai Naga bodies buried after 5 months as Naga-Kuki tensions escalate.
articles.body: Guwahati: A 24-hour general strike over the Nov 13 killing of four Tangkhul Naga civilians paralysed large parts of Manipur on Monday, with police firing tear gas to disperse protesters who blocked a road in Imphal.The shutdown coincided with the burial of six Liangmai Naga civilians at Naga Martyrs’ Park in Konsakhul village, more than five months after their beheaded bodies were recovered on June 10. The six had allegedly been abducted from Leilon Vaiphei village in Kangpokpi district on May 13.Kuki outfit slams Manipur govt, toughens stand on crisisTheir bodies had remained at the JNIMS mortuary in Imphal as their families refused to claim them until justice was delivered. The decision to proceed with the final rites was taken at a Sept 26 meeting in Guwahati involving Naga organisations, state govt representatives and the MHA.Called by the Native People’s Committee, Manipur (NPCM), the strike began at midnight and affected all five valley districts, as well as Naga-inhabited areas of Ukhrul. Markets and schools remained shut and public transport stayed off the roads, although some private vehicles operated.At Chingmeirong in Imphal East, protesters burnt tyres and demanded accountability and justice. Tensions escalated when security personnel attempted to clear the blockade. Police fired tear gas after some protesters allegedly threw stones.TheTangkhul Naga Long (TNL) separately called a 24-hour shutdown across Tangkhul areas. It blamed “Kuki terrorists”, alleged “serious lapses in security enforcement” and accused the state and central govts of failing to act against repeated targeted killings. Essential services, including electricity, water, fire, emergency and medical services, were exempted.On the Kuki side, Committee on Tribal Unity (CoTU) on Sunday cited the absence of “tangible solutions” from the state govt and adopted resolutions, including non-cooperation with all security forces in Kangpokpi district under the Senapati SP’s command, and the immediate deployment of village volunteers in fringe areas.CoTU will review “free movement” along NH-2 and govt activities if its demands don’t get a swift response.Its five-point charter, issued after the killing of two Kuki youths and a woman farmer at Taphou Kuki village, demands the removal of deputy CM Losii Dikho and action against NSCN-IM and ZUF-K. It also seeks removal of an alleged illegal NSCN-IM camp at Oklong in Senapati and withdrawal of forces under the Senapati SP from Kangpokpi. CoTU’s 48-hour shutdown in Kangpokpi ended at midnight on Nov 14.The Naga-Kuki conflict since Feb has claimed 71 lives — 38 from the Kuki community, including two pregnant women, and 33 Nagas, according to the figures provided. articles.title: Border Agents Seized and Copied an Immigration Policy Critic's Phone Without a Warrant
articles.summary: Yeah, that seems like a First Amendment violation, holds a federal judge.
articles.body:
Immigration lawyer Andrew Lattarulo doesn't just work behind the scenes. On his Instagram account —which has more than 57,000 followers—he posts videos explaining to immigrants their rights and warning them about Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations and tactics. And that, Lattarulo has argued in a federal lawsuit, is why federal agents seized his phone and copied its contents.

Sounds about right, a federal judge held last week.

Granting Lattatrulo's request for a preliminary injunction to stop the Department of Homeland Security from looking though Lattarulo's stored phone data, Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts wrote that he "is likely to succeed on the merits of this First Amendment retaliation claim."

The case starts with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and its probe of the Georges Cote law firm, where Lattarulo is a partial owner and represents clients in immigration proceedings. HSI alleged that the law firm has employed people who aren't legally allowed to work in the U.S.

In September 2025, Lattarulo and colleague Audai Cote took a weekend trip to Aruba. Upon returning to Boston, Lattarulo was stopped by Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents and an HSI officer as he deplaned. "The agents seized his cell phone without a warrant and then downloaded a complete copy of the data stored on the phone," noted Burroughs in her November 13 memorandum and order.

Warrantless cellphone searches are de rigueur for immigration agents , who claim they aren't required to adhere to the same Fourth Amendment rules as everyone else in the government. CBP policy says agents can conduct warrantless searches of electronic devices at or around the border or its functional equivalents, such as international airports, with or without suspicion. In some cases, they can also retain data from people's phones, laptops, and more.

"Seven federal appeals courts now hold that a warrant is never required to search a phone at the border, while the 4th and 9th Circuits require one in at least some cases," the Pacific Legal Foundation's Amy Peikoff noted at Reason in October. "That means one of your constitutional rights currently depends on which airport you fly into."

After seizing Lattarulo's phone at Logan Airport, officials held onto it for eight days before returning it. They also held onto his phone data—which including privileged attorney-client information, albeit in an unreadable format.

"The government intends to convert the data to an accessible format and search it if the Court permits," Burroughs explained.

Lattarulo sued, saying the search and seizure violated both his First and Fourth Amendment rights.

Lattarulo's suit alleged that he was targeted by immigration officials both because of his public political speech (such as the Instagram videos) and because of his work as an immigration attorney.

The government claimed that he was targeted because of HSI's investigation into the Georges Cote law firm.

But the government "provided no evidence that searches of cell phones are frequently conducted during the kind of employment investigation at issue here, and Lattarulo has directed the Court to sources which suggest otherwise," noted Burroughs. "The fact that the government, after Lattarulo spoke out publicly against it, elected to adopt a highly unusual investigative method that appears designed to inflict a maximal burden on Lattarulo lends substantial support to an inference that its actions were pretextual."

Burroughs pointed out that Audai Cote, who flew back to Boston a day before Lattarulo did and "had the same or greater access to the firm's employment records but did not speak publicly about immigrant rights," was not searched. Furthermore, the search happened just three days after the law firm received notice from HSI, even though the agency says employers who receive such notice have 10 business days to respond. Escalating matters after just three days by seizing an employee's phone "suggests the seizure did not arise from an ordinary investigative motive," Burroughs wrote.

Given all of this, "Lattarulo is likely to establish that he would not have been searched except for his protected speech," the judge concluded.

By granting Lattarulo's request for a preliminary injunction, she blocked the government from looking at his seized data as the case plays out, but stopped short of ordering them to destroy the data entirely.

Because the First Amendment issue was sufficient to warrant a preliminary injunction, the judge did not address the merits of Lattarulo's Fourth Amendment claim.

But she did have thoughts about what happened: "It appears that the government seized on a fortuitous border crossing following a weekend vacation as an opportunity to search for evidence of a domestic crime it was already investigating."

Surely, this can't fall within the scope of the border search exception to the Fourth Amendment—can it?

While refraining "from reaching a firm conclusion on the issue," Burroughs seems skeptical, at least, writing that "the Court is not convinced" that the exception was intended to "to apply to investigations into activity that occurred nowhere near the border and that has no relationship to the border crossing during which the search occurred. Nor is the Court convinced that application of the border search exception to this type of investigation would further the principles underlying the exception."

A 'single router in southern Arkansas' is supposedly behind the grounding of planes across the U.S. on Friday. Network gear at a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, is what "overloaded the communications system that thousands of air-traffic controllers use to guide pilots through the nation's airspace," The Wall Street Journal reports :

"We saw two places that were actually pinging our network at a very high rate, a thousand connections over every four to five seconds," Rebecca Guy, the FAA's technology chief, said at a Saturday press conference. articles.body: Customers across several of the largest banks in US ran into trouble trying to access their accounts online on Monday (November 17). According to outage tracking website Downdetector.com, users reported that services were down or experiencing issues across multiple major financial institutions and payment platforms, including Bank of America, Chase, JP Morgan, US Bank, Wells Fargo and Zelle. As per a report by AP, some Chase users trying to log in were met with an error notice stating: “Some services aren’t available. We’re working on them. Please try back later.”At the time of publishing, Bank of America customers have registered about 2100 reports while consumer banking company Chase has nearly 5000 reports of issues ranging from Account balances and transactions, web login, and transfers and wires, as per downdetector. Chase Bank’s services are experiencing a technical bug issue, not a cyber issue, AP cited a spokesperson as saying.“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible,” the Chase spokesperson said.Banking disruptions follow major Microsoft global outageThe online banking problems come on the heels of a major Microsoft outage last week that disrupted widely used services, including Outlook, Teams, and AI assistant Copilot, for hours. Microsoft has since apologised for the global disruption to its Microsoft 365 services, which took place on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and continued into Friday.Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, shared a Preliminary Post-Incident Report explaining what went wrong. We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers and recognize the impact that this has on their normal business & operations,” Lamanna said.As per the executive, the higher load and the lower server capacity together caused the gateway to hit the latent bug from July. Requests built up until the servers stopped responding. articles.title: A woman who lived with an 88-year-old millionaire for 45 years is claiming half of his £6 million mansion, alleging he promised her ownership despite never marrying her
articles.summary: An 88-year-old millionaire and his former partner are fighting over a £6 million Surrey mansion, six years after separating.
articles.body: An 88-year-old millionaire and his former partner are fighting over a £6 million Surrey mansion, six years after separating. Dennis Read and Coral Read lived together for 45 years, had three sons, and never married. Coral claims Dennis repeatedly promised the family home would be hers.She is now seeking half of Woodlands House, near Cobham, along with £215,000 in personal injury damages over alleged abuse and coercive control. Dennis denies the allegations and is separately seeking the return of £876,000 he says he transferred to Coral for their son Ashley.According to The Independent, the hearing was adjourned after half a day while Dennis undergoes a medical examination to determine whether he is fit to give evidence and to undergo cross-examination.How did Dennis and Coral's relationship lead to a £6 million family homeDennis and Coral met in late 1974 or early 1975, after both had come out of earlier relationships. Dennis was 37, and Coral was 23. At his repeated suggestion, she moved into Woodlands in December 1975. They had three sons and lived as a couple for 45 years, presenting themselves publicly as husband and wife.Coral changed her surname to Read, although they never married. The property near Cobham has since become a five-bedroom house with four bathrooms, indoor and outdoor swimming pools, and several outbuildings. The couple carried out £6 million of renovations during their relationship.Why Coral believes she is an equal owner of Woodlands HouseCoral says Dennis repeatedly assured her that he would look after her and that the house was hers. Her barrister, Noah Gifford, told the court that Dennis bought her engagement and wedding rings and said they would marry one day. Coral argues that she is an equal beneficial owner, although the property is registered solely in Dennis’s name.She is also seeking £215,000 in personal injury damages, claiming she was subjected to years of abuse and coercive control during their relationship. Her barrister said she gave up plans to return to her career and helped organised renovations. He added that Coral had used a £5,000 premium bond prize she won in the 1970s to buy a flat in her name. However, he claimed Dennis collected its rental income for decades and that the money was used to fund work on the family home.Dennis disputes her ownership and abuse claimsDennis denies that Coral is entitled to any share of the mansion and rejects her allegations of abuse and coercive control. His barrister, Marc Brittain, told the court that Dennis had owned Woodlands House before the couple met and that Coral had not contributed to its purchase.He said her role in running the household, arranging building work, decorating and buying furnishings with an allowance from Dennis did not give her a claim to ownership.His barrister also argued that Coral had received a home, financial support, private education for their children and private health cover throughout their relationship.He also challenged her claim that rental income from her flat had helped fund renovations at Woodlands, saying there was no evidence to support it. The barrister further noted that Coral had not raised allegations of abuse in her initial response to Dennis's loan claim in August 2023.The £876,000 dispute over a property owned by their sonDennis is also suing Coral for the return of £876,000, which he says he transferred to her for a specific purpose. He claims the money was meant to clear two mortgages on a property called The Lodge, on Old Lane in Cobham, which was then owned by their son Ashley. The property had been listed for sale by auction.Dennis's barrister told the court that clearing the mortgages would have allowed him to recover the land and buildings next to his home. However, this did not happen, and Dennis now wants the money back because the purpose of the transfer was not fulfilled. However, Coral denies signing the loan agreement and argues that it cannot be enforced. Her barrister says the money was a gift intended for Ashley. The hearing was adjourned after half a day, pending a medical examination to determine whether Dennis is fit to give evidence and face cross-examination.Disclaimer: This article is based on reporting by The Independent on the ongoing High Court proceedings. The Times of India has not independently verified the allegations, property ownership claims or financial arrangements disputed by the former couple. The claims mentioned in this article remain subject to the court's decision.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An Illinois couple lost their baby during childbirth in 2018 and won a $7.5 million malpractice verdict against a hospital and medical staff; on November 13, appeals judges upheld the award after a jury dispute
articles.summary: An Illinois appeals court has affirmed a $7.5 million wrongful-death verdict in favour of Jeryis and Carlos Flores, whose daughter Cianie died during
articles.body: An Illinois appeals court has affirmed a $7.5 million wrongful-death verdict in favour of Jeryis and Carlos Flores, whose daughter Cianie died during childbirth at Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center in 2018. The November 13 decision by the Illinois Appellate Court, First District, rejected the hospital and medical staff’s argument that the jury’s verdict was invalid because jurors did not have to agree on the same specific act of negligence, according to the Justia U.S. Law case record.The case involved claims that obstetrician Dr. Silvia Bicalho and nurse Josephine Jimenez failed to monitor the baby and intervene in time during labor. The appellate court found that the jury only needed to agree unanimously that each defendant was negligent and that the negligence caused the injury, not that all jurors agreed on which particular act or omission constituted that negligence. Read more details about this case, as per the record, here:What happened in 2018Jeryis Flores arrived at Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center at around 5 a.m. on September 26, 2018, in labor with her daughter, Cianie. Nurse Jimenez began caring for her at approximately 7 a.m., by which time Jeryis was nine centimeters dilated.Throughout the labor, medical staff used electronic fetal monitoring to track Cianie’s heart rate and Jeryis’s contractions. When the external monitor did not capture the fetal heart rate adequately, providers could use a fetal scalp electrode, which attaches to the fetus’s scalp and provides a more direct reading.At around 8:30 a.m., Dr. Bicalho examined Jeryis and determined that she was fully dilated but that Cianie remained relatively high in the birth canal. She instructed Jeryis to “labor down,” meaning to allow contractions and gravity to help the baby descend before actively pushing.What the experts saidPlaintiffs’ obstetrical expert, Dr. Fred Duboe, testified that Dr. Bicalho deviated from the standard of care in three ways. He said she should not have instructed Jeryis to labor down after 8:30 a.m., should have placed a fetal scalp electrode by 11:15 a.m., and should have ordered an emergency cesarean section between 12:15 p.m. and 12:20 p.m.Plaintiffs’ nursing expert, Lindsay McDevitt, R.N., testified that nurse Jimenez also deviated from the standard of care. She said Jimenez failed to question the labor-down instruction, failed to advocate for earlier placement of a fetal scalp electrode, and failed to use the nursing chain of command if Dr. Bicalho did not respond to concerns.On causation, Dr. Mark Landon, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist, testified that the tracing showed repeated umbilical-cord compression and progressive loss of fetal oxygen during the second stage of labor. He said Cianie would have survived if delivered by 12:25 p.m. and that the delay in placing a fetal scalp electrode contributed to her death.What the defence arguedThe defence presented a different explanation. Their obstetrical expert testified that Dr. Bicalho appropriately instructed Jeryis to labor down, that the fetal-heart-rate tracing did not warrant earlier placement of a scalp electrode, and that the standard of care did not require an emergency cesarean section before 12:51 p.m.Their pathologist, Dr. Ricardo Lastra, attributed the death to fetal vascular malperfusion, a condition involving reduced blood flow from the fetus to the placenta. He said the condition could not have been diagnosed before delivery.Their neonatology expert, Dr. Jeffrey Loughead, opined that a complete and unpreventable blockage of the umbilical cord occurred shortly before delivery. On cross-examination, however, he agreed that Cianie likely would have survived if delivered approximately 13 to 15 minutes earlier.The jury’s questionDuring deliberations, the jury asked whether it needed to be unanimous on one count or could be unanimous on any combination of the alleged acts or omissions. The trial court responded that jurors had to unanimously agree that each defendant was negligent but did not need to agree on which of the three possible acts constituted that negligence.Defendants argued that this response violated their constitutional right to a unanimous verdict. They said jurors could have imposed liability without agreeing that any particular act or omission was negligent or caused the injury.The trial court had relied on Galich v. Advocate Health & Hospital Corp., a 2024 Illinois appellate decision involving a similar jury question. The court told the jury it must make a unanimous decision that each defendant was negligent, but did not need to agree on which of the three possible acts constituted that negligence.What the appeals court decidedThe Illinois Appellate Court affirmed the trial court’s response. It held that a unanimous verdict required each juror to find that the defendant was negligent and that the negligence proximately caused the injury, but did not require agreement on which specific act or omission established those findings.The court explained that Illinois law treats multiple alleged departures from the standard of care as alternative bases for a single claim of liability. A general verdict can stand if at least one theory is supported by the evidence and unaffected by prejudicial error.The court also rejected the defendants’ proposed special interrogatories, which would have asked jurors whether they unanimously agreed on a particular negligent act and its causal relationship to the injury. The trial court had refused those interrogatories because it believed they would contradict the response it had already given and could lead jurors to believe they needed to agree on a specific act.Why the ruling mattersThe decision clarifies how Illinois courts handle jury unanimity in medical negligence cases involving multiple alleged acts or omissions. It confirms that jurors do not need to agree on the same specific departure from the standard of care, as long as they unanimously agree that the defendant was negligent and that the negligence caused the injury.That principle matters because medical negligence cases often involve several overlapping allegations. In this case, plaintiffs pointed to the labor-down instruction, the timing of the fetal scalp electrode, and the timing of the emergency cesarean section, among other issues.The ruling also shows how appellate courts can affirm a jury verdict even when they don’t know everything that went into it. As long as the legal standard for unanimity is met, the general verdict can stand.What it means to the Flores familyThe appellate ruling brings the Flores family a major step closer to closure. The jury’s $7.5 million award, plus costs and prejudgment interest, remains in place, bringing the total judgment to more than $9.1 million.This case highlights that although delivery is often routine, it can become dangerous if there is delay in monitoring and intervention. It also highlights the importance of expert testimony in helping juries understand complex medical decisions and their consequences.For now, the appellate court’s ruling stands. The Flores family’s claim has been upheld, and the legal question about jury unanimity has been answered in a way that supports the verdict they received.You use AI every day. articles.title: Voter or candidate has no right to get a seat reserved, says SC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday said no voter or candidate had a right to demand reservation of a particular constituency for the SC/ST community, and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday said no voter or candidate had a right to demand reservation of a particular constituency for the SC/ST community, and govt's decision to reserve a constituency could not be questioned if the number of reserved constituencies was proportionate to these communities' population.The petitioners had challenged govt's 2025 amendment to Zilla Parishads and Panchayat Samitis Act, 1961. The amendment said the next general election would be treated as the starting point for rotating constituencies reserved for SC/ST communities.They alleged this wiped out the history of previous rotations and meant some constituencies that should have been reserved based on the earlier cycle would not be reserved.Also Read| Miffed lawyer questions CJI's 'integrity', advocates seek action against himAdvocate Vipin Sanghi said, "Introduction of a new set of rules, by itself, cannot furnish an independent justification for disregarding the previous rotation cycle where relevant electoral territories substantially continue to exist, albeit with altered boundaries, areas or numerical designations,"A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked, "Do voters or candidates have a right to get their constituencies reserved for the SC/ST community?" It said, "No candidate or voter has a right to get a constituency reserved. What the rules provide for is that the number of seats reserved for the SC/ST community must be proportionate to their population in the state or democratic unit going to polls. It is nobody's case that the required percentage of seats have not been reserved for the SC/ST community."The bench refused to entertain the petition and said the amended rules conformed to the constitutionally mandated reservation policy. However, it allowed the petitioners to ask the appropriate authority to consider their representations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Kimora Lee Simmons refuses to leave a $25 million Beverly Hills mansion allegedly bought with money stolen from Malaysia's 1MDB fund; estranged husband disputes her claim to the property
articles.summary: Kimora Lee Simmons continues to live in a sprawling Beverly Hills mansion despite an ongoing legal dispute over its ownership.
articles.body: Kimora Lee Simmons continues to live in a sprawling Beverly Hills mansion despite an ongoing legal dispute over its ownership. The seven-bedroom estate, reportedly purchased in 2017 for approximately $25 million, was acquired using money that her estranged husband, former Goldman Sachs banker Tim Leissner, later admitted had been stolen from Malaysia's 1MDB sovereign wealth fund. The property was transferred in a disputed transaction in November 2020 to an entity associated with British billionaire investors David and Simon Reuben. Simmons has challenged the transaction, maintaining that it was carried out without proper authorisation. The dispute centres on the validity of the sale, the terms of a purported leaseback arrangement and who has the legal right to the property.The $25 million Beverly Hills mansion bought with 1MDB moneyThe mansion stands at 25 Beverly Park Circle, within one of Beverly Hills' most exclusive residential areas. Set across approximately 3.7 acres, the estate has seven bedrooms and became part of Leissner's property holdings after its purchase in 2017. The $25 million acquisition would later attract attention because of its connection to the 1MDB scandal, a sprawling financial fraud involving billions of dollars diverted from a Malaysian state investment fund.As reported by The New York Post, Leissner acknowledged the source of the money during testimony in 2022, when he appeared as a government witness in the criminal trial of his former Goldman Sachs colleague Roger Ng in Brooklyn. He told the court that the money used to purchase the house had been taken from the Malaysian fund. Simmons has not been accused of participating in the fraud. Her legal representatives have also stated that she had no knowledge of the scheme and did not receive money connected to it.Kimora Lee Simmons challenges the validity of the mansion saleThe ownership dispute centres on a transaction involving a company connected to Leissner and a group of entities associated with the property's subsequent owners. According to court documents cited by the New York Post, the mansion was transferred in November 2020 to the Reuben brothers after payments relating to a $12 million mortgage fell into difficulty.The transaction reportedly involved a sale-and-leaseback arrangement. Under its terms, Leissner and Simmons were expected to pay $65,000 a month to remain in the property. However, the validity of the agreement has become a major point of contention. Simmons maintains that she never consented to the transaction and disputes the signature attributed to her on the relevant paperwork. In a filing connected to the case, she alleged that her signature had been forged and that she had neither authorised its use nor known about the document.Her position is that the purported sale was unauthorised and therefore invalid. Her lawyers have also disputed the suggestion that she owes rent to the current owners, arguing that any lease arrangement arose from a transaction that she considers void. They have said she has spent substantial sums maintaining the estate and keeping its property taxes up to date.The Reuben brothers' ownership claim and the unpaid rent allegationsDavid and Simon Reuben, British billionaire brothers with extensive real estate interests, became associated with the property through the 2020 transaction. Court filings indicate that the arrangement followed difficulties with the mortgage, while a source familiar with the deal told the New York Post that part of the loan proceeds had been used to cover Leissner's personal living expenses.The question of rent has added another layer to the dispute. According to the newspaper's reporting, Simmons has continued occupying the mansion since November 2020 without making the monthly payments contemplated under the agreement. The Reuben brothers have declined to comment publicly on the matter. Simmons' legal team, meanwhile, maintains that she has never been under any obligation to pay rent because she did not approve the transaction that purportedly created that obligation.The couple no longer live together, according to sources cited in the report. They share a son, who was reported to be 10 years old at the time of publication. Leissner had previously testified that he continued living at the property after his 2018 arrest, although he did not establish precisely when he moved out.How the mansion became connected to the 1MDB scandalThe property dispute has its roots in one of the largest international financial scandals of recent decades. The 1Malaysia Development Berhad fund was established in 2009 to support Malaysia's economic development. Investigators later uncovered a complex network through which billions of dollars were diverted from the fund and moved through international financial institutions, companies and luxury asset purchases.Malaysian financier Jho Low was identified by investigators and prosecutors as a central figure in the scheme. He used money linked to the fraud to acquire expensive properties, fund an extravagant lifestyle and make purchases associated with celebrities and other wealthy individuals. Leissner, who worked at Goldman Sachs, played a significant role in the financial arrangements surrounding the fund and eventually pleaded guilty to offences connected to the scandal in 2018.The Beverly Hills mansion was among the assets purchased with the diverted money. Its subsequent ownership arrangements have attracted particular attention because several other properties associated with the fraud were seized by US authorities. Leissner's testimony also raised questions about attempts to move assets through corporate structures before they could be pursued by investigators.Why the property has not been forfeited like other 1MDB-linked assetsThe mansion's legal position differs from that of several other luxury properties acquired with money from the scheme. US authorities pursued civil asset forfeiture proceedings against numerous assets linked to 1MDB, including expensive residences in New York and Los Angeles.One example was a condominium on Columbus Circle in Manhattan, purchased by Low for approximately $30.55 million. Another was a penthouse in Manhattan's Walker Tower, acquired in 2014 for around $51 million by Khadem al Qubaisi, a former Abu Dhabi official implicated in the scandal. The US government seized the latter property and sold it in 2020 for approximately $18 million.The Beverly Hills estate, however, was not forfeited as part of those proceedings. Its subsequent transfer through companies connected to Leissner and the later buyers has left questions about its ownership and the possibility of further claims against it. Sources quoted by the New York Post suggested that Malaysia could still seek to recover the property or pursue other assets acquired with misappropriated funds.The wider recovery effort has already resulted in substantial sums being returned to Malaysia. The US Department of Justice has reported recovering approximately $1.4 billion in assets connected to the scandal, making the case one of its largest international asset-recovery efforts.Leonardo DiCaprio and other celebrities returned gifts linked to the fraudThe 1MDB investigation also reached the entertainment industry after authorities traced some of the money to gifts and luxury purchases involving well-known personalities. Actor Leonardo DiCaprio was among those who returned items received from Low after their connection to the fund came under scrutiny.These included works by Pablo Picasso and Jean-Michel Basquiat, together valued at approximately $12.2 million, as well as an Oscar statuette originally awarded to Marlon Brando. The items were among the assets surrendered as part of the US government's efforts to recover money connected to the scandal.Simmons' name has also appeared in reporting about the wider circle surrounding the scandal, partly because of her previously discussed friendship with Rosmah Mansor, the wife of Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak. However, there is no allegation that Simmons received gifts purchased with stolen 1MDB money or participated in the financial scheme.Mansor's own collection of luxury goods became a subject of public attention in 2018, when Malaysian police seized hundreds of handbags from properties associated with the former prime minister. The collection included hundreds of luxury pieces, many of them stored in their original packaging. Some were subsequently returned, while others were sold by the authorities.Kimora Lee Simmons' reality television return continuesAway from the courtroom proceedings, Simmons has returned to television with Kimora: Back in the Fab Lane, bringing viewers into her family life and business activities. The reality series also offers a glimpse of her extensive luxury handbag collection.In a promotional clip, she describes herself as a luxury hoarder while showing off a collection that reportedly numbers 698 bags, including Hermès Birkin pieces. The collection has attracted attention in part because of the comparisons made between her interest in designer accessories and Mansor's well-documented accumulation of luxury handbags. There is, however, no evidence linking Simmons' collection to the 1MDB funds.The Beverly Hills mansion dispute remains a separate matter from her television appearances. A trial-setting conference was scheduled for February 25, 2026, as the long-running civil proceedings continued. Leissner, who surrendered to federal prison in Pennsylvania on February 6, 2026, following his guilty plea in the 1MDB case, had not actively participated in the property proceedings at the time of the New York Post report.For now, the future of the estate remains tied to the unresolved legal claims. Simmons continues to dispute the validity of the sale, while the competing parties seek clarity over title, possession and financial responsibility for the property.You use AI every day. articles.title: Lauren Sánchez has a Bell 429 helicopter she affectionately calls ‘her baby’; the former TV journalist also holds fixed-wing and helicopter licences and runs an aerial production company that films Blue Origin rocket launches
articles.summary: Lauren Sánchez has spent much of her career in front of cameras, first as a television journalist and later as a familiar figure in the world of business,
articles.body: Lauren Sánchez has spent much of her career in front of cameras, first as a television journalist and later as a familiar figure in the world of business, entertainment and philanthropy. Away from public appearances, however, she has maintained a connection with aviation that began long before her relationship with Amazon founder Jeff Bezos attracted international attention. Sánchez is a qualified helicopter pilot who has built a professional interest around flying and aerial filming. She has even taken journalists aboard her aircraft, offering a glimpse into a side of her life that rarely receives as much attention as her high-profile relationship.Sánchez's early career in television and her family roots in aviationBefore aviation became a defining part of her professional identity, Sánchez established herself in broadcast journalism. She worked in television news and became particularly familiar to viewers through her time on Fox 11's Good Day LA. Her interest in flying, though, was not simply a later addition to her career. Aviation had been part of her family background. Her father was a pilot and mechanic who owned a flight school, while her mother also held a pilot's licence. Growing up around people familiar with aircraft gave Sánchez an early connection to the field.She eventually obtained a fixed-wing pilot's licence before undertaking further training to qualify as a helicopter pilot. The two qualifications involve different types of aircraft and flying skills, and her decision to pursue both gave her a route into aerial production as well as personal flying.Lauren Sánchez’s Bell 429 helicopter and her passion for flyingDuring the interview at Bezos's sprawling West Texas ranch, Sánchez took the journalist towards a Bell 429 helicopter. Her introduction to the aircraft was affectionate and direct. In an interview with Vogue, she called it her baby, making clear that it was something she particularly enjoyed showing off.The aircraft was more than an accessory to her life with Bezos. Sánchez was comfortable discussing helicopters, describing their appearance and capabilities with the enthusiasm of someone who had spent considerable time around them. She also demonstrated that her flying experience extended beyond occasional recreational trips.During the Vogue visit, she took Malle on an aerial tour of the Texas property, accompanied by a co-pilot named Zeus. Sánchez flew for much of the journey, giving the journalist a view of the enormous desert landscape from above. The ranch, which the profile described as covering more than 400,000 acres, includes the Blue Origin facilities used for the company's space-related operations.The flight also offered a practical illustration of how aviation fits into Sánchez's daily activities. She was not simply being transported around the property. She was at the controls, navigating the aircraft while discussing the surrounding landscape and the previous day's photography shoot.The aerial production company behind her work with Blue OriginSánchez's involvement with helicopters eventually developed into a business venture. After her television career, she established an aerial production company, creating another professional outlet for her aviation qualifications.Her connection with Blue Origin has also given the business a role in documenting spaceflight. According to Vogue's 2023 profile, Sánchez's company films all of the aerospace company's launches. This places her aviation work in a different setting from the film industry, with cameras capturing rockets as they leave the ground rather than aircraft moving across conventional landscapes.The work requires a combination of planning, technical coordination and an understanding of aerial operations. Filming a rocket launch is not the same as shooting a conventional film sequence. The timing is tied to the launch schedule, while the aircraft and camera teams must operate within the necessary safety restrictions.Her involvement with Blue Origin extends beyond the cameraHer professional association with Blue Origin has also brought her into the company's wider activities. Sánchez was present when Bezos travelled aboard the company's first crewed New Shepard flight in July 2021. articles.title: In 1963, John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr lived together in this London building; a flat directly below their former home is now listed for £4.5 million
articles.summary: A three-bedroom London flat in the Mayfair building where all four Beatles lived together in 1963 has entered the property market for £4.5 million.
articles.body: A three-bedroom London flat in the Mayfair building where all four Beatles lived together in 1963 has entered the property market for £4.5 million. The apartment is located directly below the top-floor home once shared by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, during the only period when the four lived under one roof.According to Mansion Global, the band’s manager, Brian Epstein, leased the former home, known as Flat L, for the group. The building provided privacy as crowds of fans began following the Beatles after the success of their second UK No. 1 single, ‘She Loves You’, according to listing agency Wetherell. The property for sale has been recently renovated and covers almost 1,300 square feet.How did the Beatles’ shared London home become famousThe Beatles’ former home was on the top floor of the building on Green Street, in Mayfair. Their manager, Brian Epstein, leased Flat L for the four musicians in 1963. It was the only time John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr lived together. The address gave the band privacy as their popularity grew and fans began following them after ‘She Loves You' became their second UK No. 1 single.The building featured in early Beatles publicity. A photograph showing the four looking over the banister in its stairwell appeared on the cover of the December 1963 edition of The Beatles Book. Their stay together did not last long, and each member moved elsewhere in London.How long did the Beatles live together in their London homeThe Beatles lived together in the building for only a short period. By the end of 1963, Lennon had moved to an apartment in Kensington with his wife, Cynthia, and their son, Julian. McCartney moved in with Jane Asher’s family in Marylebone. Harrison and Starr kept the Green Street flat briefly as a bachelor pad after Lennon and McCartney had left. They then relocated to Knightsbridge in early 1964. The building therefore marked a brief chapter in the group’s shared history, rather than a long-term base.Inside the £4.5 million flat in the Beatles’ former buildingThe apartment currently on the market is on the floor directly below the Beatles’ former home. The recently renovated property spans almost 1,300 square feet and has three bedrooms. It was brought to the market in August by the estate agency Wetherell.Mansion Global reported that the seller could not be identified, while property records showed that the flat was last traded for £2.4 million the previous year. The asking price is £4.5 million, equivalent to US$5.9 million. The home is in the same building that housed the band in 1963, but it is a separate apartment from the top-floor Flat L leased by Epstein for the four musicians.Three-bedroom flat features open-plan living space and marble interiorsAn entrance hall leads into the flat’s open-plan living, kitchen and dining area. The main space has four sash windows and ornate plasterwork. The kitchen is fitted with walnut cabinetry and Carrara marble countertops. The three bedrooms include a primary suite, which has a separate dressing area and a marble bathroom. Reportedly, there were few buildings in London with a genuine claim to Beatles history, and fewer that combined that history with an interior-designed apartment finished to this standard. The flat’s location directly beneath the former Beatles home is central to its connection with the band in Mayfair, London.Disclaimer: This article is based on reporting by Mansion Global and property details provided by estate agency Wetherell. articles.title: At Sonia's book launch, Gandhis open up about love, loss, and bad chicken
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: \"And listen, if you want to fall in love, go to Varsity Restaurant in Cambridge.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: "And listen, if you want to fall in love, go to Varsity Restaurant in Cambridge. But never eat the chicken chasseur, okay?" Rahul Gandhi jokingly delivered this piece of advice at the launch of his mother Sonia Gandhi's memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love', in Delhi on Monday. Years after hearing the story about his parents' first meeting in Cambridge, he recounted how he went to the Varsity Restaurant with his girlfriend to see where they had met.When Rahul told the man at the entrance that his parents had met there, the man said he knew exactly who they were and recommended the chicken chasseur from the menu. However, the meal did not live up to its romantic legacy. Rahul contrasts his parents' memories of the restaurant with his own experience. "They seem to remember that the food was fantastic. The food's horrible!" he said as the audience laughed.The anecdote was part of a series of family recollections the leader of the opposition shared after saying he had been instructed to avoid politics. However, many read a political subtext into the seating arrangements. In the front row was an array of opposition leaders such as Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav; Trinamool Congress MP Abhishek Banerjee; National Conference president Farooq Abdullah; Supriya Sule of NCP-SP; Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren; and Tamil Nadu CM C Joseph Vijay. Also in the front row was former Punjab CM Captain Amarinder Singh, who left Congress in 2021 following a bitter falling-out with the Gandhis.Rahul name-checked Amarinder and mentioned that he had seen his parents fight only once. Rajiv Gandhi was speaking to Amarinder on phone when Sonia tried several times to tell him something. Rajiv was stressed and eventually got angry. "We saw them argue many times, but that was the only time we ever saw them fight," Rahul said.Sonia Gandhi too kept the conversation away from politics. Asked why she chose to write a memoir when she had guarded her privacy fiercely in the past, she said she wanted to set the record straight about her family amid "unreal stories" woven around them. "So much has been said about my mother-in-law, husband, son, daughter, and myself; and most of it is unreal. It has really nothing to do with the way we are. Stories are woven around you, untruths are woven around you, and hurtful things are said which are nowhere near the truth. And I thought, well, perhaps this was a way of bringing out my feelings, what I know of my family, and maybe people will be open to listening to my story too," the Rajya Sabha MP said.She recalled feeling like an outsider when she first moved to India, conscious of making mistakes. She connected that experience to Indian women who enter a new family after marriage and have to adjust to its ways. The memoir's title, she said, reflected "the effort to be accepted and to belong, to finally belong."While she recounted a story of how she and Rajiv would go to India Gate to have ice cream (she had a favourite Sardarji ice cream vendor), Rahul spoke of his parents' affection and a habit he had assumed was common in every home: "Every meal there would be Papa and on Papa's lap there would be Mama." He said he realised it was unusual only when he visited friends' homes.But things changed after the assassinations of Indira Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi, he said, "The fun-loving mother, the smiling mother disappeared." Sonia, once an extrovert, withdrew into herself.Rahul also spoke of his mother's resilience in the face of cancer, saying he had never seen her afraid or back down. He ended by telling her how proud he believed Rajiv would have been of her: "Mummy, Papa loved you. But I cannot even tell you how proud he would be of you."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Tom Cruise surprises British man who completed a 31-mile ice-skating marathon, climbed the height of Mount Everest and walked 94 miles to honour his late twin cousins
articles.summary: Tom Cruise surprised a British fundraiser who spent a year pushing himself through extreme sporting challenges to honour his late twin cousins and support
articles.body: Tom Cruise surprised a British fundraiser who spent a year pushing himself through extreme sporting challenges to honour his late twin cousins and support seriously ill children. Lloyd Kembrey, a facilities manager at the University of Bristol, was expecting a routine interview when the Hollywood actor walked into the room and thanked him for his efforts. As reported by The Independent, Kembrey’s fundraising journey included a 31-mile ice-skating ultramarathon in Finland, climbing the equivalent height of Mount Everest on a climbing wall and walking 94 miles along the Jurassic Coast in southern England.Tom Cruise surprised Lloyd Kembrey after his fundraising challengesThe unexpected meeting was organised by the BBC’s The One Show as part of its One Big Thank You initiative, with help from Kembrey’s family and the Jessie May team. According to Jessie May’s account, Kembrey had travelled to London believing he was being interviewed for a documentary about endurance sport and fundraising.The interview took place at Raffles London, inside the former war office of Winston Churchill. Kembrey later told The Independent that he had even looked up the hotel’s room prices and realised it was an unusually expensive setting for an interview.About 20 minutes into the conversation, Cruise entered the room. Kembrey initially mistook the actor for musician James Blunt, before the crew cheered and the surprise became clear.Cruise explained that he had heard about Kembrey’s extraordinary adventures and wanted to meet him personally. The actor, known for performing demanding stunts in his films, said he had undertaken many wild experiences himself but was impressed by Kembrey’s determination to raise money for others.The encounter was more than a brief congratulations. Cruise invited Kembrey to attend the royal film performance and world premiere of his upcoming film Digger, giving the fundraiser another unexpected experience following his year of challenges.What inspired the endurance challengesKembrey’s fundraising was rooted in a deeply personal family story. His twin cousins, Francesca and Josephine, were diagnosed with Sanfilippo disease type A, a rare and fatal genetic condition, when they were three-and-a-half years old. Both died in their teens.The Independent reported that Kembrey wanted to honour their memory while helping other families dealing with life-limiting diagnoses. Jessie May had supported his cousins and remained an important part of his family’s life, making the charity a natural focus for his efforts.The organisation provides specialist nursing care to children with life-limiting conditions and supports their families. Its nurses help children receive care at home, where families can spend time together in familiar surroundings.Kembrey’s connection with the charity stretches back to childhood. Jessie May said he had been involved in fundraising from a young age, with his family taking part in activities to support the organisation before he became an official ambassador.Difficulty of these sporting featsThe challenges Kembrey undertook were designed to test his physical endurance and determination. The 31-mile ice-skating ultramarathon in Finland was among the most demanding, requiring him to cover a long distance on ice in difficult conditions.Another challenge involved climbing the equivalent height of Mount Everest on an artificial climbing wall. Rather than scaling the mountain itself, he accumulated the height through repeated climbing, turning the famous peak into a sustained indoor endurance task.He also completed a 94-mile walk along the Jurassic Coast in southern England. The route added another major physical test to a year already filled with demanding activities.The Independent described these feats as part of a year-long series of extreme athletic challenges undertaken to raise funds for Jessie May. The challenges were not limited to these three headline achievements. His fundraising programme also included other endurance events, reflecting a sustained effort rather than a single sporting undertaking.How much did the fundraising help Jessie MayAccording to The Independent, the money raised enabled Jessie May to provide practical support to children and families facing serious illness.Former Jessie May chief executive Daniel Cheesman praised Kembrey’s contribution, explaining that the funding allowed the charity to support children in their own homes. He also described him as a role model for the children and young people receiving its care.Kembrey’s aunt and uncle, Julie and Chris, whose daughters were Francesca and Josephine, also appeared in a video message during the programme. They expressed their pride and thanked him for everything he had done in their daughters’ memory.What happened after the surprise meetingKembrey later attended the premiere of Digger with a friend, according to The Independent. He also appeared in another segment of The One Show alongside Cruise and met actors including John Goodman, Riz Ahmed and Jesse Plemons.Reflecting on the encounter, Kembrey said Cruise was genuinely lovely and recalled that the actor had suggested taking a selfie together. He admitted he might otherwise have forgotten to ask for one himself.Jessie May reported that the surprise offered a chance to recognise the fundraiser's dedication and bring attention to the charity's work.You use AI every day. articles.title: United Airlines hit by system outage days after nationwide ground stop; issue resolved within hours
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: United Airlines on Monday resolved a technology outage that disrupted departing flights across its network in the US, just days after a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: United Airlines on Monday resolved a technology outage that disrupted departing flights across its network in the US, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) telecommunications system triggered a nationwide ground stop.The Chicago-based airline said it was troubleshooting a technical issue affecting its departure operations. While several flights were delayed, aircraft already in the air and flights operated by its regional network, United Express, remained unaffected."There is no indication that this is a cybersecurity-related issue," United said in a statement, ruling out any immediate signs of a cyberattack. The airline also apologised to passengers for the inconvenience caused by the disruption.The issue was resolved approximately 1.5 hours after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.What caused the United Airlines outage?Although United did not immediately disclose the precise nature of the technical failure, reports indicated that the problem affected multiple applications used by pilots, including systems for crew communications and aircraft departure calculations.An internal memo issued by United's pilots union, seen by Reuters, said a company-wide web-based outage had disrupted several applications used by pilots.The airline was unable to provide final aircraft weight calculations for departing flights. These figures are essential for pilots to determine whether an aircraft meets the required safety parameters before takeoff.The memo advised pilots to follow instructions from airport station personnel on whether to remain at their gates.A recording shared on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking air traffic controllers for permission to remain at the gate until the airline's systems were restored.The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual tracking of aircraft.Some passengers also reported on social media that their aircraft had reached the runway before returning to the gate following the technical disruption.How many flights were affected?According to flight-tracking website FlightAware, United had delayed 418 flights, accounting for around 13% of its scheduled operations, and cancelled 21 flights as of 5:30 pm ET (2230 GMT) on Monday.However, the figures did not establish how many of these disruptions were directly linked to the technology outage.The FAA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Outage comes days after nationwide US ground stopThe United Airlines disruption came as US aviation operations were recovering from Friday's nationwide ground stop, which lasted nearly five hours following a failure in the FAA's telecommunications network.The malfunction involved a newly installed router that overwhelmed the ageing air traffic control system, prompting the FAA to temporarily halt all flights.The disruption affected thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays and cancellations across the country.According to aviation analytics firm Cirium, more than 18,100 flights scheduled to depart US airports between Friday and Sunday were either cancelled or had not taken off within three hours of their scheduled departure times. However, not all these disruptions were necessarily linked to the FAA outage.The latest United incident was also part of a series of technology disruptions affecting major US companies.Earlier on Monday, thousands of customers reported difficulties accessing their online accounts at several major US banks following a technical problem at JPMorgan Chase.A day before that, Microsoft experienced a major disruption to its Outlook email service. The company said on Saturday that services had been fully restored.The back-to-back incidents have brought renewed attention to the dependence of critical services, including aviation, on interconnected computer systems, where technical failures can disrupt operations even when aircraft, pilots and airport infrastructure are available.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran planning dirty bomb attack in Washington, US intel warns
articles.summary: US intelligence indicates that Iran is developing contingency plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington, DC, using a
articles.body: US intelligence indicates that Iran is developing contingency plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington, DC, using a radioactive dirty bomb or chemical weapons, CNN reported, quoting seven US officials familiar with the intelligence.The intelligence points to specific potential locations and targets in the US capital, prompting American authorities to step up contingency planning. However, officials told CNN that the reported preparations do not necessarily indicate an imminent attack or a decision by Tehran to execute such a plot.The White House said the administration was monitoring potential threats but maintained that there was no immediate credible threat to the US mainland.In a statement, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said that the US is “monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.”According to CNN, US officials view the intelligence as a possible indication that Tehran is considering escalating the conflict beyond the Middle East as it faces continued American military pressure and an economic blockade.“Whether they actually have the personnel in place to execute is a matter of debate,” one of the sources told CNN.Two officials told CNN that several meetings had been held over the past week to discuss measures to counter the potential threat. One source described the preparations as “prudent”.The reported intelligence comes amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the conflict between Washington and Tehran. US President Donald Trump said last week that the war would be over “fairly soon”, even as tensions continued around the Strait of Hormuz.What US intelligence says about Iran's alleged plansCNN reported, quoting sources familiar with the intelligence, that American officials are concerned about Tehran's willingness to consider attacks inside US territory. However, officials remain divided over whether Iran has the personnel and operational capability to carry out such an operation.One of the sources told CNN that US intelligence had picked up Iranian communications suggesting that bomb-making materials may have been stored inside the United States. Officials are reportedly divided over the credibility of this information.CNN reported, quoting sources, that some American national security officials believe radioactive materials or chemical agents capable of being used in an attack could already have been positioned inside the country.“As porous as our border has been for the better part of ten years, it would have been extremely easy to get operatives inside the country” who could acquire and place bomb components, one source close to the intelligence told CNN.Another source told CNN that Iran's ability to carry out such an attack had not necessarily increased, but its incentive to consider one may have changed.The reported concerns come against the backdrop of previous Iranian plotting against current and former American officials. CNN reported that such activities have continued since Trump's first administration and have largely focused on targeting US officials while they were travelling overseas.These included an alleged murder-for-hire plot against Trump in 2024.Follow Iran War Live Updates:What is a dirty bomb and how dangerous can it be?A dirty bomb is a conventional explosive device designed to spread radioactive material over an area. Unlike a nuclear weapon, it does not rely on a nuclear fission reaction and does not produce a nuclear explosion.Although a dirty bomb is considerably less destructive than a nuclear weapon, it can disperse radioactive material and contaminate surrounding areas, creating public health and security concerns.The immediate casualties from such an explosion would generally result from the conventional blast, while the radioactive material could create additional contamination risks.A source familiar with the latest intelligence told CNN: “Any weapon like that is a weapon of terror, not a weapon of precision, just like a suicide bomber blowing themselves up,” the source said. “They can make people really sick and certain areas uninhabitable.”According to CNN, American officials believe that acquiring radioactive material would be one of the main challenges in assembling such a device.The US intelligence assessment has also raised questions about the country's ability to detect potential plots before they are carried out.US surveillance capabilities and security concernsThe reported threat comes amid uncertainty over a key US surveillance law that allows authorities to collect communications involving foreign nationals.The law expired in June following a political standoff between the White House and Congress. Surveillance orders approved before its expiry remain valid until March 2027, but national security officials have warned that the loss of the provision could weaken their ability to identify potential terrorist plots.CNN reported that Attorney General Todd Blanche, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA Director John Ratcliffe wrote to Republican and Democratic leaders of both chambers last week, urging them to reauthorise the law.In their letter, the officials argued that delays would “(put) the lives of both Americans in the homeland and our troops stationed abroad at risk in the heightened threat environment briefed to the Gang of 8.”The Gang of 8 comprises the four congressional leaders and the bipartisan leadership of the House and Senate Intelligence Committees.CNN reported that the lawmakers had received a briefing on Iran several days before the letter was sent. However, it remains unclear whether the briefing specifically covered the alleged dirty bomb or chemical weapons threat to Washington.The Defense Department referred questions to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which declined to comment.The Iranian Mission to the United Nations in New York rejected allegations involving chemical weapons but did not directly address the reported intelligence about a potential dirty bomb plot.In a statement, an Iranian Mission spokesperson said Iran “considers the use of chemical weapons under any circumstances to be wholly illegitimate and categorically rejects and unequivocally refutes the false and fabricated allegations circulated in this regard.”Separate concerns over chemical attacks on US troopsApart from the reported threat to Washington, American intelligence agencies are also monitoring information suggesting that Iran could consider using chemical weapons against US troops stationed in the Middle East, CNN reported, quoting two US officials.The New York Times had earlier reported concerns about a possible chemical weapons threat to American forces.According to CNN, several US officials have raised concerns that American troops may not have adequate protective equipment or training to respond to such an attack.The intelligence has prompted a separate contingency planning exercise focused on ensuring that American diplomatic and intelligence personnel in the region have the necessary protective equipment and training.One source familiar with the latest intelligence told CNN that preparations were underway to protect personnel in the event of an Iranian chemical weapons attack.US-Iran conflict and growing regional tensionsThe reported threats come as Washington and Tehran remain locked in a conflict centred around the Strait of Hormuz, with diplomatic efforts to end hostilities and lift the American blockade yet to produce a breakthrough.Although sources in the region believe both sides are interested in reaching an agreement, neither has so far appeared willing to make major concessions.A regional source told CNN that the coming weeks would be critical for negotiations and warned that certain groups could attempt to derail any potential agreement.The source identified Iranian hardliners and rogue elements within the regime as possible spoilers, suggesting that groups that have benefited from the conflict could have an incentive to launch an attack to prolong hostilities.A US official told CNN that Iranian leaders understand the consequences of using chemical or radioactive weapons against American targets, including the possibility of a retaliatory response from Washington.However, the official cautioned that if Iran's leadership begins to view the survival of its regime as being at stake, it could consider taking risks that would otherwise be unacceptable.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Indiana woman who has owned her home since 1989 sued neighbours after they shifted a fence by about a foot in 2022, claiming the grassy strip between their properties; an appeals court ruled the land was not hers
articles.summary: A fence moved by about a foot became the centre of a property dispute between neighbours in Indiana, where a homeowner claimed ownership of a grassy strip
articles.body: A fence moved by about a foot became the centre of a property dispute between neighbours in Indiana, where a homeowner claimed ownership of a grassy strip separating their properties. The woman, who had owned her house since 1989, argued that the land belonged to her despite the neighbouring owners' decision to install a replacement fence in 2022. However, the Indiana Court of Appeals ruled against her, finding that she had not established the legal requirements to claim the disputed property.In its November 13, 2026, memorandum decision in Deanne Ellen Gloppen v. Daniel Goldfarb, available on Justia, the appeals court affirmed a lower court ruling in favour of the neighbouring property owners. The judges examined whether Gloppen could establish ownership through adverse possession, a legal principle that can allow someone to acquire another person's land after meeting specific conditions over a required period. The court concluded that her evidence did not satisfy those conditions, particularly the requirement concerning property taxes.Dispute began after neighbours moved the fenceGloppen has owned and lived at her home at 304 Elmhurst Street in Valparaiso, Indiana, since 1989. The neighbouring property at 306 Elmhurst Street has belonged to Daniel and Julia Goldfarb since 2007. The disagreement concerned a grassy strip along the boundary between the two properties. In 2022, the Goldfarbs removed an existing fence and installed a replacement. The new fence stood approximately six to eight inches north of the deeded property boundary and about one foot south of the previous fence.According to the court record, at least three fences had been erected along that side of the Goldfarbs' property over time, and they had not all occupied the same position. In October 2022, Gloppen filed a lawsuit seeking ownership of the disputed strip through adverse possession. The Goldfarfs opposed her claim and asked the court to recognise their ownership under their property deeds. In June 2025, Gloppen filed a motion for summary judgment, asking the court to establish the boundary between the two properties. After a hearing, the trial court denied her motion and granted the Goldfarfs' cross-motion. She subsequently appealed the decision.Court examined adverse possession requirementsThe Indiana Court of Appeals considered whether Gloppen had demonstrated the legal elements necessary to establish adverse possession. Under Indiana law, a person claiming land through adverse possession must establish four elements by clear and convincing evidence: control, intent, notice and duration. The claimant must exercise control over the property, demonstrate an intention to claim it as their own, make that claim sufficiently visible to notify the legal owner and maintain the possession continuously for at least 10 years.There is also a separate tax requirement. A claimant must pay the property taxes and special assessments attributable to the disputed land that they reasonably and honestly believe are due. The court found that Gloppen had not established this requirement. She had not provided sufficient evidence that she reasonably believed her property tax payments covered the grassy strip.During the summary judgment proceedings, her lawyer acknowledged that Gloppen paid taxes on the property described in her deed, while the Goldfarfs paid taxes on the property covered by theirs. The judges clarified that adverse possession does not necessarily require a separate tax assessment for the disputed land. However, the claimant must demonstrate a reasonable, good-faith belief that their tax payments cover the property they are attempting to acquire.The court also considered the evidence concerning the fences and the use of the disputed area. Gloppen had not claimed that she maintained or replaced the fences, nor had she demonstrated improvements to the strip that would have alerted the neighbours to an ownership claim.Appeals court upheld the lower court rulingGloppen also relied on an earlier Indiana decision involving a fence that had been mistakenly treated as a property boundary. However, the appeals court explained that the Indiana Supreme Court had subsequently disapproved of that decision's interpretation of the tax requirement.She additionally appeared to raise an argument based on boundary acquiescence, a legal principle that can apply when neighbouring owners recognise and follow an incorrect boundary for at least 20 years. However, she had not included this claim in her amended complaint and could not introduce it for the first time during the summary judgment proceedings.On November 13, 2026, the Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's decision, leaving ownership of the disputed grassy strip with the Goldfarfs. The ruling was issued as a memorandum decision under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D). It is not binding precedent for other courts and may generally be cited only for persuasive purposes or in limited circumstances.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
