articles.body: At 5 am, while much of the city is still asleep, a group of teenage girls is already on the training ground in Mohali. Their mornings begin with physical exercises, followed by school or college classes. The afternoons bring military drills and coaching, while their evenings are reserved for preparing for competitive examinations. By 8.30 pm, when most teenagers might be relaxing, these girls return to their rooms with books and notebooks. They continue studying until 11 pm. Mobile phones are switched off after 10 pm.For the cadets at Punjab's Mai Bhago Armed Forces Preparatory Institute for Girls, this demanding routine has a clear purpose: to earn a place at the National Defence Academy (NDA) and pursue a career in the Indian Armed Forces. Their hard work recently brought an encouraging result. Seventeen cadets from the institute in SAS Nagar, Mohali, cleared the NDA written examination in 2026. According to the institute, this is its highest-ever number of successful candidates and the largest number of female qualifiers from a government institution in the country.Among them is 17-year-old Khushi from Beas, whose father works as a gardener at a military station in Pathankot. Her journey reflects how determination, family support and access to the right opportunities can help young girls pursue ambitions that once seemed difficult to achieve.A campus where discipline begins before sunriseEstablished by the Punjab government in 2015, the Mai Bhago Armed Forces Preparatory Institute is named after Mai Bhago, also known as Mata Bhag Kaur, the legendary Sikh warrior. The residential institution was created to prepare young women from Punjab for careers as commissioned officers in the Armed Forces. After the NDA opened its doors to women in 2022, the institute introduced a dedicated NDA Preparatory Wing in 2023. It currently has 115 female cadets, including 40 in the NDA Wing and 75 in the Graduate Wing.Life on campus follows a carefully structured schedule. Physical training begins at 5 am, followed by academic education. After returning from school or college, the girls attend evening drills and coaching sessions. The institute also provides facilities such as a gymnasium, shooting range, sports grounds and an obstacle course designed to prepare candidates for the physical demands of military training. The evening study hours are equally important. Cadets are expected to remain focused on their preparation between 8.30 pm and 11 pm, with staff monitoring their study routine.Meet Khushi, the gardener's daughter with an Army dreamAmong the 17 girls celebrating their written examination success is Khushi, a 17-year-old from Beas in Punjab's Majha region. Her father, Vijay Kumar, works as a gardener at a military station in Pathankot. Growing up around military personnel, Khushi developed an interest in joining the army herself. Her family supported her aspirations. With the help of army officers, her father arranged for her admission to Army Public School.Khushi later discovered Mai Bhago Institute through social media. Getting into the institution was not easy. She had to clear a selection process that included a written examination and an interview. After earning her place, she began preparing for the NDA examination alongside her academic studies and physical training.Now that she has cleared the written examination, her attention has shifted to the next stage: the Services Selection Board (SSB) assessment, which evaluates a candidate's suitability for becoming a defence officer. Speaking about her aspirations, Khushi expressed hope that she would eventually realise her dream. She also credited the institute for giving her the opportunity and encouragement to pursue it.17 girls clear the NDA written examinationKhushi is not alone in this achievement. Seventeen cadets from the institute successfully cleared the all-India NDA written examination, making it the largest successful batch in its history. The achievement is particularly significant because women account for only around 6 per cent of the NDA's seats, compared with 94 per cent for men. The institute has described the result as a record for a government-run institution, including Sainik Schools and Rashtriya Military Schools.For the girls, however, clearing the written examination is only one step towards their larger goal. They must now prepare for the SSB assessment and meet the remaining selection requirements. The institute's director, Major General J.S. Sandhu, has highlighted the importance of preparing the cadets for both their education and the demands of military service. The Punjab government provides boarding, lodging, uniforms and training at the institute, while students bear their school and college education expenses.More than an examination resultThe institute's achievements extend beyond this year's NDA results. Since 2022, 68 of its 128 lady cadets have been recommended for commissioning into the Armed Forces, according to its director. For young women like Khushi, such opportunities can make a significant difference. Her father's profession does not define the limits of her ambitions, and her family's support has helped her take the first steps towards a career she has dreamed of since childhood.The institute's demanding routine, from early morning physical training to late-night study sessions, reflects the commitment required to compete in a highly challenging selection process. Khushi also has a message for other girls who wish to enter the Armed Forces: dare to dream and work towards making those dreams a reality. articles.title: US judge strikes down Trump rule restricting stays for foreign students, journalists
articles.summary: A US federal judge on Monday struck down a Trump administration rule that sought to impose fixed periods of stay on foreign students, exchange visitors
articles.body: A US federal judge on Monday struck down a Trump administration rule that sought to impose fixed periods of stay on foreign students, exchange visitors and international journalists, ruling that the policy was arbitrary and not in accordance with the law.District Judge F Dennis Saylor vacated the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) final rule under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), granting a summary judgment in favour of the plaintiffs and rejecting the US government's request to uphold the policy.The court held that the administration had failed to adequately justify the restrictions, assess their potential costs and benefits, or demonstrate that they were necessary to prevent immigration fraud and protect national security."For the foregoing reasons, and the reasons set forth in the Memorandum and Order on Motion for Preliminary Injunction dated September 14, 2026, plaintiffs’ motion for summary judgment is GRANTED and defendants’ motion for summary judgment is DENIED," the order signed by District Judge F Dennis Saylor read."The Final Rule, entitled Establishing a Fixed Time Period of Admission and an Extension of Stay Procedure for Nonimmigrant Academic Students, Exchange Visitors, and Representatives of Foreign Information Media, 91 Fed. Reg. 44976 (July 17, 2026), is hereby VACATED pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 USC. § 706," it added.Which visa categories were covered by the rule?Published in the Federal Register on July 17, 2026, the rule sought to establish fixed periods of admission and a new extension-of-stay procedure for several categories of non-immigrants.It covered international students holding F-1 visas, researchers, professors and instructors under J-1 visas, and foreign journalists and media representatives holding I visas.The policy would have replaced the existing duration-of-status framework with fixed periods of stay, requiring affected foreign nationals to seek extensions under a new system.The court had previously issued a preliminary injunction on September 14, 2026, postponing the implementation of the rule under Section 705 of the APA. The US government subsequently appealed that decision before the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit. The appeal was still pending when the latest order was issued.Why did the court strike down the rule?The court found that DHS had failed to adequately evaluate the potential consequences of the policy or provide sufficient evidence to support its claims that the restrictions were necessary to tackle fraud and national security concerns.It also questioned whether the department had properly considered less restrictive alternatives and addressed concerns raised during the public consultation process.A key issue was the existing Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), which allows authorities to monitor international students and exchange visitors through reporting and data collection by educational institutions.The plaintiffs argued that DHS should have considered making greater use of SEVIS before introducing a new system. They pointed to the responsibilities of Designated School Officials (DSOs) and Responsible Officers (ROs), who report information about foreign students and exchange visitors.The court noted that DHS had previously strengthened SEVIS, including implementing recommendations made by the Government Accountability Office in 2019. These measures included identifying fraud involving institutions seeking certification, verifying the eligibility of DSOs and developing a risk-assessment model.The department had also used SEVIS records to identify suspected abuses, investigate 'pay-to-stay' fraud and refer potential violations to field offices for further examination. It had additionally checked the records of more than one million students against the National Crime Information Centre to identify individuals whose behaviour could indicate fraudulent visa overstays.DHS, however, maintained that SEVIS was a 'data-reporting system for schools, not an immigration-status adjudication system'.The court rejected the department's justification, observing that it had not adequately explained how introducing a discretionary renewal system after a foreign student had already spent four years in the US would improve its ability to identify fraud.It also said DHS had failed to establish how the benefits of the proposed system would outweigh the costs of abandoning the existing framework.Court flags restrictions on academic mobilityThe judge also examined whether the proposed restrictions were consistent with the Immigration and Nationality Act, particularly Section 1101(a)(15)(F), which governs the F-1 student visa category.The provision allows a 'bona fide student' who qualifies to pursue a full course of study to enter the US temporarily for that purpose.DHS had argued that the department's secretary had the authority to determine what constituted an appropriate course of study and could consequently impose restrictions on certain academic programmes.However, the court observed that the department's interpretation could prevent foreign students from pursuing extended academic programmes, including PhD courses, joint degrees, changes in academic specialisation and programmes that were not at a higher academic level than their previous qualifications.Referring to the 2022 ruling in Washington Alliance of Technology Workers v. United States Department of Homeland Security, the court said Congress had reserved the authority to establish the terms of entry while delegating to the executive branch the power to determine the duration and conditions of non-immigrants' stay in a manner reasonably connected to the purpose of their visa category.The judge concluded that DHS's stated objectives of preventing fraud and protecting national security were not reasonably connected to the purpose of the F-1 visa programme."Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity—providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States—that Congress sought to permit and encourage," the court observed."The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program," it added.Who challenged the Trump administration's rule?The legal challenge was brought by a coalition of higher education, labour and media organisations.The plaintiffs included the Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers, Graduate Labour Organisation (AFT Local 6516), The NewsGuild-CWA, International Union, United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America, and United Auto Workers Local 2322.The organisations challenged the administration's proposed changes, arguing that the existing monitoring framework provided mechanisms to address concerns over immigration fraud and national security without imposing additional restrictions on foreign students, researchers and journalists.You use AI every day.
